metadata.title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

problem.value: Learning effective visual representations without human supervision is difficult.

evidence.quote: Learning effective visual representations without human supervision is a long-standing problem.

problem.value: Pixel-level generation methods are computationally expensive and potentially unnecessary for representation learning.

evidence.quote: However, pixel-level generation is computationally expensive and may not be necessary for representation learning.

problem.value: Heuristic-based pretext tasks can restrict the generality of learned representations.

evidence.quote: Many such approaches have relied on heuristics to design pretext tasks (Doersch et al., 2015;Zhang et al., 2016;Noroozi & Favaro, 2016;Gidaris et al., 2018), which could limit the generality of the learned representations.

contributions.value: The introduction of SimCLR, a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations.

evidence.quote: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations.

contributions.value: A systematic study of the major components of the proposed contrastive learning framework.

evidence.quote: In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework.
This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations.

method_summary.value: SimCLR uses a stochastic data augmentation module to transform data examples into two correlated views considered as positive pairs.

evidence.quote: A stochastic data augmentation module that transforms any given data example randomly resulting in two correlated views of the same example, denoted xi and xj , which we consider as a positive pair.

method_summary.value: A base encoder network, such as ResNet, extracts representation vectors from the augmented data examples.

evidence.quote: A neural network base encoder f (•) that extracts representation vectors from augmented data examples.

method_summary.value: A small neural network projection head with a nonlinear MLP maps representations to the latent space where the contrastive loss is applied.

evidence.quote: A small neural network projection head g(•) that maps representations to the space where contrastive loss is applied.

method_summary.value: The framework optimizes the model using the normalized temperature-scaled cross entropy loss (NT-Xent).

evidence.quote: This loss has been used in previous work (Sohn, 2016;Wu et al., 2018;Oord et al., 2018); for convenience, we term it NT-Xent (the normalized temperature-scaled cross entropy loss).

method_summary.value: The model is trained using large batch sizes and the LARS optimizer, along with global batch normalization across all distributed devices.

evidence.quote: To stabilize the training, we use the LARS optimizer (You et al., 2017) for all batch sizes.

novelty.value: The authors note that most individual components have appeared in previous work, and the improved performance stems from the specific combination of design choices.

evidence.quote: As we have noted in the main text, most individual components of SimCLR have appeared in previous work, and the improved performance is a result of a combination of these design choices.

claims.value: A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet.

evidence.quote: A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by Sim-CLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-ofthe-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50.

claims.value: Fine-tuning on only 1% of the labels achieves 85.8% top-5 accuracy.

evidence.quote: When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100× fewer labels.

claims.value: SimCLR outperforms previous work while remaining simpler without specialized architectures or a memory bank.

evidence.quote: Not only does SimCLR outperform previous work (Figure 1), but it is also simpler, requiring neither specialized architectures (Bachman et al., 2019;Hénaff et al., 2019) nor a memory bank (Wu et al., 2018;Tian et al., 2019;He et al., 2019;Misra & van der Maaten, 2019).
